regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY looks unambiguous until you note that the RBI's own forecast sits 110bps lower at 6.7% YoY — a gap that historically reflects deflator assumptions, not real output divergence. PMI Composite at 55.9 and IIP at 8.0% YoY corroborate momentum, but core sector at 4.8% YoY (down from 5.0%) is the goods economy's honest confession. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — a 18-month high — is the one number that makes the growth story credible: you don't invest at 77% unless you believe 80% is coming.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY is 44bps above the RBI's upper tolerance band, but the decomposition is what matters: fuel at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, a 10-year high) is doing most of the damage, while core CPI at 3.9% YoY sits at the 28th percentile — structurally benign. The inversion: if the RBI cuts on the back of low core, it validates a narrative that fuel inflation will self-correct; if Brent holds above $110/bbl, that bet fails and the second-order effect is a forced reversal into a weakening rupee. WPI at 9.92% YoY is already flashing the pipeline pressure that CPI will absorb in two quarters.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposit growth of 17.8% YoY is a 160bps divergence that has widened for two consecutive months — the CD ratio at 81% has eased from 83% but remains at the 73rd percentile historically. The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% while the repo rate was being held was FY14; within 12 months, external shocks forced emergency tightening. NBFC credit accelerating to 15.8% YoY (from 10%) is the second-order risk: NBFCs fund at the margin, and if deposit competition pushes bank funding costs up 25-50bps, NBFC spreads compress before their loan books reprice.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, but the real rate calculus has shifted: with CPI at 5.54% YoY, the real repo rate is effectively negative 29bps — accommodative by accident, not design. The RBI's own inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY implies they expect relief; Brent at $113.43/bbl and food inflation at 7.74% YoY suggest that relief is not imminent. For housing, the average home loan rate at 7.35% p.a. means affordability is already stretched; any upward repo adjustment would push EMIs on a ₹80 lakh loan up ₹2,200/month — enough to tip the mid-segment buyer back to renting.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (up from 16.1%) with capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is the most internally consistent signal in today's data: firms expand capacity when utilisation approaches 80%, and we are 260bps away. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile, up from 10.3%) confirms the investment is not confined to manufacturing. The inversion: if credit tightening materialises — whether via RBI macro-prudential action or deposit competition forcing banks to ration — the capex pipeline stalls precisely when the order books are fullest. Core sector at 4.8% YoY is the early warning: infrastructure inputs are not accelerating at the same pace as capital goods orders.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month is at the 73rd percentile and stable, but the composition matters more than the headline: passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY have decelerated for two consecutive months (from 26.1%), while two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY rebounded sharply. That divergence — mass-market rural mobility recovering while urban discretionary cools — is the informal economy's signal that the consumption recovery is broadening downward, not narrowing upward. Commercial vehicle sales at 12.6% YoY (falling two months in a row from 28.9%) are the freight economy's honest read: goods movement is slowing even as the PMI suggests expansion.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1% → 19.4% credit; 9.9% → 17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY), now at 57th percentile.","implication":"RBI will face pressure to tighten liquidity or signal rate cuts to ease deposit mobilisation. Banks with CASA ratios > 45% will outperform; avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities. Overweight private banks with strong deposit franchises (HDFC, Kotak). Underweight PSU banks dependent on RBI liquidity windows.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level. Historically, ratios above 85% preceded NBFC stress (2018–19); current 81% signals tightening but manageable if deposit growth sustains.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadens Beyond Cyclicals","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest, up from 16.1% YoY), now at 52nd percentile. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%), at 74th percentile — highest in 18 months. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5% YoY but stable). Credit to industry at 18.2% YoY, services credit surging at 24.3% YoY (up from 10.3% YoY, 79th percentile).","implication":"Capex cycle is real but uneven: manufacturing capex is solid, but services credit explosion (IT, telecom, logistics) suggests GCC expansion and infrastructure outsourcing, not traditional capex. Overweight capital goods (Cummins, Timken, Xylem), industrial automation (Bosch, ABB), and logistics (TCI Express, Allcargo). Avoid pure-play construction plays; they're not seeing the capex uptick.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is near the 10-year median; historically, sustained levels > 80% preceded 2–3 years of strong capex. Current momentum suggests we're in early innings of a 2–3 year upcycle.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit 93rd Percentile, But Ticket Size Inflates","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (latest), rising 3 consecutive months (₹29,845 → ₹31,961 → ₹32,297 → ₹32,490 cr / month), at 93rd percentile. SIP accounts at 10.06 mn (down from 10.45 mn, at 2nd percentile — data quality issue). SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (up from ₹16.64 lakh cr, 89th percentile). Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (up from ₹29,329 cr / month, 80th percentile).","implication":"SIP inflows are strong, but average ticket size is rising (SIP AUM +7.3% vs SIP accounts flat/declining) — this is affluent money entering, not mass retail. Retail is rotating into equities from debt. Overweight large-cap quality (Nifty 50 constituents with 20%+ ROE). Avoid micro-cap SIP plays; they're not the buyer. Watch for SIP account growth to stabilise — if it doesn't, the affluent money is crowding out new retail entrants.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile are near all-time highs. Historically, such levels preceded 6–12 month equity rallies but also marked late-cycle behaviour (2021, 2017). Monitor SIP account growth closely; if it decelerates, it signals saturation among affluent cohorts.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation at 95th Percentile, CAD Risk Rising","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest, up from 20.05% YoY), at 95th percentile — highest in 10 years. Brent crude at $113.43/bbl (down from $117.64/bbl but up 4 of last 5 months from $110.8/bbl). WTI at $104.12/bbl (flat, 85th percentile). FAO food index at 136 index (up from 134.5, 61st percentile). India's headline CPI at 5.54% YoY (up from 4.83% YoY, 52nd percentile), food inflation at 7.74% YoY (up from 5.97% YoY, 57th percentile).","implication":"Oil and food inflation are the primary drivers of headline CPI overshoot. RBI will struggle to cut rates until fuel inflation moderates. Current oil prices ($110–115/bbl) imply a 3–4% drag on CAD if sustained. Hedge INR weakness via long USD positions or short INR forwards. Overweight energy stocks (ONGC, Reliance) for dividend yield; avoid consumer discretionary. Reduce exposure to import-heavy sectors (autos, chemicals).","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a 10-year high. Historically, such spikes preceded 6–9 month periods of RBI hawkishness and INR weakness. Current spike is driven by global oil, not domestic policy — RBI has limited tools.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"BOJ Tightening Threatens Carry Trade Unwind","data_text":"BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (up from 1% p.a., at 100th percentile — highest in 10 years), rising 2 consecutive months (0.75% → 1% → 1.25% p.a.). Fed funds at 3.75% p.a. (up from 3.63% p.a., 68th percentile), rising 2 in a row. ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (up from 2.25% p.a., 63rd percentile), rising 2 in a row. US 10Y Treasury at 4.98% yield (down from 5.05%, but 90th percentile). US PMI composite at 58.4 index (up from 56, 91st percentile).","implication":"BOJ tightening is the tail risk. Carry trades funded in JPY are unwinding — this will pressure INR, emerging market equities, and high-beta sectors. FII flows to India are already negative (₹-49,935 cr / month net, 17th percentile). Reduce leverage, hedge JPY exposure, and avoid illiquid EM assets. Overweight defensive sectors (pharma, FMCG, utilities). Watch for VIX spikes > 20; they signal carry unwind acceleration.","pct_10y":100,"pct_note":"BOJ at 100th percentile is a structural shift — Japan is exiting ultra-loose policy for the first time in 20 years. Historically, BOJ tightening cycles preceded 12–18 month periods of EM volatility and JPY strength.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakens to 95.24, FII Outflows Accelerate","data_text":"INR/USD at 95.24 ₹ (up from 94.95 ₹, at 89th percentile — near 10-year weakness), up 2 of last 5 months from 94.34 ₹. FII equity net outflows at ₹-49,935 cr / month (latest, at 17th percentile — severe outflow). DII equity net inflows at ₹51,829 cr / month (at 95th percentile), offsetting FII outflows. India VIX at 15.3 index (down from 15.3, at 10th percentile — complacency).","implication":"INR weakness is structural: FII outflows are accelerating due to BOJ tightening and US rate stickiness. Overweight domestic-demand plays (banks, FMCG, real estate).","pct_10y":89,"pct_note":"INR at 89th percentile weakness is near 10-year lows. Historically, such levels preceded 3–6 month periods of RBI intervention and eventual stabilisation, but only after 2–3% additional depreciation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Rents Surge While Absorption Collapses — GCC Arbitrage","data_text":"Office absorption at 15.08 mn sq ft / quarter (latest, at 8th percentile — lowest in 10 years), down from 24.6 mn sq ft / quarter 5 months ago. Office vacancy at 14.8% vacant (at 43rd percentile, stable). Yet Bengaluru office rents at ₹168.75 ₹/sqft/mo (up from ₹151.5 ₹/sqft/mo, at 99th percentile — 10-year high), and Mumbai office rents at ₹342.58 ₹/sqft/mo (up from ₹329.25 ₹/sqft/mo, at 100th percentile — all-time high). Retail mall vacancy at 4.8% vacant (at 7th percentile — tight), down from 5% vacant.","implication":"Traditional IT services are consolidating (absorption down), but Global Capability Centers (GCCs) and non-IT corporates are paying premium rents for prime locations. This is a structural shift: IT services are no longer the marginal buyer of office space. Real estate investors should pivot from IT-dependent assets to GCC-friendly, mixed-use properties in Bengaluru and Mumbai. Nifty IT stocks are not a proxy for commercial real estate demand — they're inversely correlated now. Overweight office REITs (Embassy, Mindspace) only if they have GCC tenants; avoid those with >40% IT services exposure.","pct_10y":8,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 8th percentile is a 10-year low, yet rents are at 99–100th percentile highs. This divergence signals a structural reallocation: GCCs and non-IT corporates are replacing IT services as the marginal tenant. If IT absorption continues to fall while rents stay elevated, it confirms GCC displacement — a 3–5 year structural headwind for IT services real estate.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP, But the Goods Economy Is Losing the Thread

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY — up from 7.4% YoY — with PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) and IIP at 8.0% YoY confirm broad expansion.
  • Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, 18-month high) is the structural anchor: private capex follows utilisation, not budget speeches.
  • But core sector at 4.8% YoY (down from 5.0%) and commercial vehicle sales falling to 12.6% YoY for two consecutive months signal goods-economy deceleration beneath the headline.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY rebounding while passenger vehicle sales slow to 7.9% YoY (two consecutive months of deceleration) maps a consumption recovery that is widening to rural mass-market, not deepening in urban discretionary.

The tension: GDP and PMI point up; core sector and CV sales point sideways. The RBI's own forecast of 6.7% YoY — 110bps below the print — implies the statistical gap between headline and real output is doing meaningful work.

Bottom line: Watch core sector YoY: a third consecutive month below 5.0% YoY would signal that infrastructure inputs are not validating the capex narrative.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

DM Re-acceleration Meets BOJ's Slow Tightening Fuse

The facts:

  • US GDP SAAR accelerated to 3.4% SAAR (rising three consecutive quarters from 0.7%) and US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile) — the strongest DM growth signal in two years.
  • But US 10Y Treasury at 4.98% yield (90th percentile) is tightening financial conditions faster than the Fed is — real economy stress is embedded in the curve, not the policy rate.
  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, rising two consecutive months from 0.75%) is the underappreciated tail: every 25bps of BOJ tightening unwinds yen carry trades that have funded EM equity positioning for three years.
  • Eurozone GDP at 1.2% YoY (up from 0.6%) with CPI at 3.8% YoY (rising two consecutive months) means the ECB at 2.5% p.a. is not done — synchronised DM tightening is the base case, not the risk case.

The tension: DM growth surveys are re-accelerating while nominal GDP growth in the US is still below the 10Y yield — bond markets are tightening for central banks. BOJ is the mechanism by which this resolves into EM outflows.

Bottom line: BOJ at 1.50% p.a. is the threshold: a third consecutive hike would trigger measurable yen carry unwind and test India's FII positioning within 30–60 days.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Autopilot Holds, But Institutional Conviction Is Absent

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile, rising three consecutive months) with SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (89th percentile) — retail flows are structurally anchored.
  • Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (80th percentile, up from ₹29,329 cr / month) confirm domestic institutional absorption is active.
  • But FII equity net outflows at ₹-49,935 cr / month (17th percentile — severe) are being absorbed almost entirely by DII inflows of ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) — a one-for-one offset that leaves no margin.
  • NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile, 10-year low) signal that fund managers are not launching new products — institutional conviction in fresh deployment is absent even as SIP autopilot runs.

The tension: Retail SIP flows are at record highs; institutional product launches are at decade lows. DII absorption is covering FII exits to the rupee — any acceleration in FII selling breaks the equilibrium.

Bottom line: If FII outflows sustain above ₹50,000 cr / month for a second consecutive month, DII absorption capacity will be tested and Nifty support at 22,700 becomes the line to watch.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Mumbai Rents at All-Time Highs, Absorption at 8th Percentile — REITs Price the Wrong Signal

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 20% (up 2pp), with 25% share within premium/luxury; Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Hyderabad are the primary destinations, supported by remittances at $144.8 bn (16.2% YoY).
  • Mumbai office rents at ₹342.58/sqft/mo (100th percentile, all-time high) and Bengaluru at ₹168.75/sqft/mo (99th percentile) — but office absorption at 15.08 mn sq ft / quarter sits at the 8th percentile.
  • GCCs now account for 41% of office occupier demand; Hyderabad absorption surged 92% YoY and NCR 106% YoY — the rent spike is a GCC concentration story, not broad-based demand.
  • But Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, and Brookfield at ₹263/unit are all down 10–28% from prior prints — REIT unit prices are pricing absorption weakness, not rent strength.
  • Residential: Hyderabad leads with sales 15% YoY and launches 120% YoY; NCR sales at -1% YoY despite prices up 12% YoY — the affordability ceiling is visible in the data.

The tension: Prime office rents are at all-time highs in Mumbai and 10-year highs in Bengaluru, yet REIT unit prices have fallen 10–28% — the market is discounting that GCC-driven rent spikes in a handful of micro-markets cannot sustain portfolio-level distributions when aggregate absorption is at decade lows.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until absorption recovers above 20 mn sq ft / quarter; overweight Hyderabad and Bengaluru residential developers with NRI-facing premium inventory.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Fuses, One Detonator — BOJ Is the Sequence

The facts:

  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, third hike in three months) — yen carry unwind threatens FII positioning in Indian equities; FII outflows already at ₹-49,935 cr / month.
  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, 10-year high) with Brent at $113.43/bbl — every $10/bbl adds ~$15 bn to India's annual import bill and widens CAD by ~40bps, pressuring INR at 95.24 ₹ (89th percentile).
  • CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits with credit at 19.4% YoY vs deposits at 17.8% YoY — if deposit competition forces funding costs up 25–50bps, NBFC spreads compress before loan books reprice.
  • US CPI rising three consecutive months to 3.72% YoY with core PCE at 3.12% YoY — if the Fed resumes hiking from 3.75% p.a., the DXY strengthens and INR depreciation accelerates the CAD-inflation feedback loop.

The tension: Each risk is individually manageable; the sequence — BOJ hike → yen carry unwind → FII outflows → INR depreciation → fuel import cost spike → RBI forced to tighten — is the scenario that none of the individual risk monitors will catch in time.

Bottom line: Watch BOJ's next policy meeting: a rate at 1.50% p.a. or above triggers the carry unwind sequence and is the single most important data point this week.

"}
